idiom_name: function-pointer hook table with register/unregister (notifier-chain style)
implementation_notes: C has no framework to hook into, so the full structure is hand-written: a chain or array of entries holding a callback pointer plus an opaque service context, register/unregister functions, and a dispatch point that the framework side calls per event (the Linux kernel's notifier chains - struct notifier_block with notifier_call, register_netdevice_notifier, blocking_notifier_call_chain - are the canonical example of exactly this idiom). The classic abstract Interceptor class is replaced by the callback signature and a void* user pointer, and the Context role by a struct that the framework fills in and passes to every hook. Services that live in a shared object can attach themselves at load time via dlopen/dlsym plus a constructor function; the dispatcher must copy or lock the list because a callback may unregister itself during dispatch.
pitfalls: A callback that unregisters or frees its own entry during dispatch invalidates the list walk: snapshot the chain, use intrusive safe-unlinking, or defer removal until dispatch returns.
The void* service context defeats the type system; keep the event struct frozen and versioned, because every hook compiled against an older layout still sees it.
Ownership is undefined by default: agree who frees hook state, and only dlclose a shared object after its hooks have been deregistered, or a later event calls into an unmapped page.
Concurrency is the caller's problem: register/unregister versus dispatch needs a lock (or RCU/atomic publish) once more than one thread can emit events.
